```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
library(bssd)
```

```{r helpers, include = FALSE}
read_results <- function(folder, name) {
  read.csv(system.file(folder, "results", name, package = "bssd",
                       mustWork = TRUE), stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}
fmt <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
count_of <- function(tab, j) sum(tab$judgement == j)
```

Waterhouse et al. (2022) describe how a safety management team uses BDRIBS
(`vignette("bdribs1")`) in ongoing blinded trials: a contour plot of the
posterior probability \(P(RR > 1)\) over the numbers of events and the
patient-years of exposure prepared before the first patient enters the
trial, a sensitivity analysis over the background rate, and pooling of
blinded data from several trials with different randomization ratios. The
examples use a fixed background rate and the Jeffreys prior Beta(0.5, 0.5)
for \(p\).

## Contour plot

Example 1 of Waterhouse et al. (2022): MACE with a background rate of 3.1
events per 100 patient-years and randomization 1:1.

```{r grid}
g <- bdribs_grid(y = 4:10, exposure = seq(40, 240, by = 10),
                 lambda_hp = 0.031, p_prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
z <- matrix(g$prob, nrow = 7)
contour(4:10, seq(40, 240, by = 10), z, levels = c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9),
        xlab = "Number of events", ylab = "Patient-years of exposure")
```

The probabilities for six and seven events (Figures 3 and 4):

```{r ex1}
subset(g, y %in% 6:7 & exposure %in% c(80, 100, 140))
```

## Sensitivity to the background rate

With 10 events in 200 patient-years, the probabilities at the limits of the
90% credible interval of the background rate from 496 events in 15,730
patient-years (Figures 5 and 6) are

```{r sens}
bg <- qgamma(c(0.05, 0.95), 496, 15730)
bdribs_grid(y = 10, exposure = 200, lambda_hp = bg, p_prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
```

The background rate can also be given a Gamma prior instead of a fixed
value (`pt_hp` in `bdribs_post()`).

## Pooled trials

Example 3: trial A with 250 patient-years at 1:1 and trial B with 80
patient-years at 2:1 are pooled; the effective randomization ratio is the
ratio of the expected exposures on study drug and on control.

```{r pool}
k <- pooled_ratio(c(250, 80), c(1, 2))
k
bdribs_post(y = 16, exposure = 330, k = k, lambda_hp = 0.031, pt_hp = Inf,
            p_prior = c(0.5, 0.5))
```

## Reproduction of Waterhouse et al. (2022)

```{r repro, include = FALSE}
w <- read_results("reproduce", "reproduce_Waterhouse2022.csv")
w <- w[w$judgement != "INFO", ]
```

`inst/reproduce/reproduce_Waterhouse2022.R` compares the probabilities,
exposures and the pooled randomization ratio given in the text and figures
(`r count_of(w, "PASS")` PASS, `r count_of(w, "FAIL")` FAIL). The published
values were read from an R Shiny application that samples by MCMC; the
tolerance is 0.01 for probabilities given in percent and 0.02 for those
given as "about" (the other tolerances are in the table).

```{r repro-table, echo = FALSE}
knitr::kable(data.frame(quantity = w$quantity, published = w$published,
                        bssd = fmt(w$reproduced), tolerance = w$tolerance,
                        judgement = w$judgement), align = "lrrrl")
```

## References

Waterhouse, B., Hartford, A., Mukhopadhyay, S., Ferguson, R. and
Hendrickson, B. A. (2022). Using the Bayesian detection of potential risk
using inference on blinded safety data (BDRIBS) method to support the
decision to refer an event for unblinded evaluation. *Pharmaceutical
Statistics*, 21(2), 372--385. <https://doi.org/10.1002/pst.2175>
